Drag to orbit · wheel to zoom · shift-drag to pan · 1–9 or S stage a fault · Run button plays · Space pauses.
Mid-cut, one closed-loop X motor on each end plate pulls the gantry along its rack. The two must stay in step.
Chips packed in the far rack: the far pinion rides up out of the teeth and skips. (End plate removed to show it.)
The driver sees the lag only after 1.8°: the far end plate trails and the bridge racks out of square. Green is where it should be.
Correction fails: the driver trips, its LED turns red, input 4 turns red on the screen and every axis stops where it is.
The clip stays clamped on the carriage plate (plate → spindle → collet → bit); Z-zero plate under the bit; input 1 must light on contact.
C2 brings the bit down and it touches the plate — but the lead is broken inside its coil: the circuit stays open.
No contact signal: Z keeps pushing. The brittle cutter shatters and throws sharp fragments before the plate visibly bends. Illustrative slow motion; spindle off.
Input 1 never lit on the screen. The bit has shattered. E-stop, wait for all movement to stop and call staff; inspect and replace the cutter before re-zeroing.
C3 homing: the gantry runs toward X 0 until the target on its end plate passes the proximity switch.
The target sweeps right over the switch — misaligned, the switch never changes state and inputs 2 and 3 stay as they were.
With no signal the gantry overruns the switch and slams into the hard stop at the end of the rail.
The motors stall against the stop and the driver trips. Inputs 2 and 3 never changed; the position the software shows is now wrong.
Start on the pendant was pressed after OK, so output 1 never switched the spindle on. The VFD reads 0 Hz.
The file runs anyway: the still bit plunges into the sheet at 20 mm/s.
Feeding sideways, a bit that isn't turning cannot cut: it drags and bends.
…and snaps.
Pass 1, 9 mm deep. Only the friction of the ER25 collet holds the bit. A tick on the nut lines up with a tick on the shank.
Pass 2, 18 mm deep, twice the load: the whole bit — shank top and all — creeps down out of the nut. Green is where it should be.
Pass by pass it keeps sliding. The encoders notice nothing: every motor is exactly where it should be. Only the bit has moved.
Cut open: the floor of the groove steps deeper with every pass, toward the spoilboard. The extra depth is drawn ×4.
Final pass, cutting through. The clamps hold the edges of the sheet — nothing holds the part itself: no tabs, no screws.
The freed part lifts along the edge nearest the bit.
Its edge catches the bit: the part kicks up and spins on the cutter.
Flung off the table in a fraction of a second — and the bit snaps. Never reach for a loose part while the tool moves.
Chips packed between the teeth of the near rack.
Each time the pinion rides over a chip it skips a few steps; the gantry falls a little short. Green is the commanded position.
The second pass (red) lands offset from the first (dark): the error accumulates with every move.
The part comes out stepped and undersize; the machine still believes it is in the right place.
The PC streams the file to the control box over USB, one move at a time, while the spindle cuts.
The PC dozes off, a plug works loose or noise hits the cable: the USB link drops, the screen freezes and the gantry stops dead mid-cut.
The file has stopped; the spindle has not. E-stop is the only control that still kills it.
E-stop on the pendant cuts spindle power at once — the frozen screen cannot. Then re-home: the position is lost.
Between profiles the bit rapids across the sheet at the CAM clearance height: 15 mm above the surface.
Ahead stands a clamp whose knob tops out 48 mm above the sheet — far higher than the bit is lifted.
At 760 mm/s the bit strikes the knob: the clamp is torn sideways and the bit bends.
The X motors stall against the clamp; their driver trips an alpha fault, input 4 turns red and everything stops.
Screws hold the waste down to the spoilboard. A screw gets hit when the CAM clearance height is set below its head, or when it is placed on the toolpath — like this one, on the profile line.
Spindle running, the bit feeds along the profile at 60 mm/s, straight at the screw head. Green is the toolpath from CAM: it runs right across the screw.
Impact at full speed: the brittle carbide tip shatters and throws fragments; the screw head is gouged and knocked over. Illustrative slow motion; tilt exaggerated.
Aftermath: a broken shank in the collet, a chipped screw and carbide fragments on the sheet. The spindle is still running until you stop it.
